entities.name: Raskolnikov and Sonya
entities.short: A proud former student nursing a dangerous idea, and the daughter of a drunken clerk whom he first knows only from her father’s confession. Dostoevsky sets them side by side as two answers to the same poverty: one tries to calculate his way out of it, the other gives herself away to save her family.

compare.a: A former law student who left the university for lack of money and hides from his landlady in a garret under the roof.
compare.b: The daughter of the clerk Marmeladov by his first marriage, living with a consumptive stepmother and starving little children.

compare.a: He turns his own destitution into a theory: in the tavern talk he hears that one death may buy a hundred lives and takes it as a sign.
compare.b: She leaves the house after her stepmother’s reproach and comes back with thirty roubles, silently laid on the table: a sacrifice, not a theory.

compare.a: He refuses to accept his sister’s sacrifice for him and thinks of Sonya as the measure of such sacrifices.
compare.b: She is the sacrifice others accept: her father drinks away the money she earns and confesses it in a tavern.

compare.a: In the dream of the beaten horse he rushes to kiss its muzzle and is horrified by his own thought of murder: for that moment his own mind rejects what he has planned.
compare.b: By her father’s account she goes out onto the street for the hungry children and pays with herself, not with another’s life: she has no idea of a right behind it, and so she can be read as the counterweight to his plan.

entities.bonds: One reading: both are crushed by the same Petersburg poverty, and both do what the world forbids. Raskolnikov himself sets his case against Sonya’s: reading his mother’s letter, he measures his sister’s sacrifice by her fate (chapter 4).
entities.differences: In Part One the difference is in the motive: he nurses his deed for an idea and to test himself, she sacrifices herself for her family and proves nothing to herself.

quotes.text: Sonia, Sonia Marmeladov, the eternal victim so long as the world lasts.
quotes.interpretation: Reading his mother’s letter, he measures his sister’s marriage by Sonya’s fate: for him Sonya is the image of a sacrifice he refuses to accept.

entities.conclusion: The pair can be read as the book’s central question put from two sides: may a person step over another for an idea. Raskolnikov’s calculation and Sonya’s uncalculated sacrifice show two answers to the same poverty.

faq.question: Why does Dostoevsky compare Raskolnikov with Sonya?
faq.answer: Both are pushed by poverty to cross a forbidden line, which lets the author contrast a crime committed for an idea with a sacrifice made for others.
